claims.reason: S1 directly defines checkpointing as transferring WAL transactions into the database.
S1 explicitly lists reading, writing, and checkpointing as the three WAL primitive operations.
S2 states this nonwaiting procedure and conditional database sync. It does not explicitly state both busy-handler behavior and possible incompletion required by the passive rubric entry.
S2 supports the busy-handler rule and the precise concurrency condition that can leave the checkpoint unfinished.
S2 supports the waiting conditions and subsequent checkpoint and sync. The claim omits continued admission of new readers, so it does not fully state the full rubric entry.
S2 connects the additional database-only reader condition to the next writer restarting the log.
S2 explicitly specifies RESTART behavior plus truncation to zero bytes before successful return.
S2 supports zero checkpointed frames and retrieval of log and checkpointed-frame status through output parameters.
S1 states interface exclusivity for FULL and RESTART only. S2 documents TRUNCATE through this interface but does not establish the claim's exclusive initiation restriction for TRUNCATE.
S1 supports both triggers and the 1000-page unit. Threshold-triggered checkpointing and final-connection cleanup are independently applicable facts.
S3 supports the post-commit threshold of N frames. The claim does not specify configuration scope on one connection.
S3 explicitly states that non-positive N disables automatic checkpointing.
S1 and S3 explicitly identify automatic checkpoints as PASSIVE.
S3 supports the callback conflict and resulting replacement of automatic checkpointing. The claim omits the reverse replacement direction required by hook-replacement.
S1 explicitly limits concurrent checkpoint progress at any active reader's end mark, preventing transfer of later WAL pages.
S1 specifies storage of checkpoint progress in the wal-index and resumption on the next invocation. This does not state the lookup and host restriction covered by wal-index.
S1 explicitly identifies a long-running read transaction as a condition that can stall checkpoint progress. It does not state overlapping-reader starvation and WAL growth.
S1 directly connects continuously overlapping readers to checkpoint incompletion and unbounded WAL growth.
S1 supports complete transfer, synchronization, and absence of WAL readers as the conditions permitting rewind. The claim does not assert that rewind occurs immediately.
S1 explicitly describes ordinary WAL reuse from the beginning instead of truncation.
S1 supports the final-connection cleanup sequence of checkpointing and deleting both files. Its deletion specifics distinguish it from f10.
S1 supports WAL growth degrading reads and checkpoint scheduling mitigating that effect. The claim omits the increased WAL lookup cost specifically required by read-amplification.
S1 specifies both synchronization ordering constraints and their role in avoiding corruption after power loss or hard reboot.
S1 explicitly attributes slower checkpoints to synchronization and seeking overhead. This is a causal performance mechanism without an additional conditional tradeoff.
S1 supports the checkpoint-frequency tradeoff between read performance and amortized write cost. The write-side consequence distinguishes it from f22.
S1 explicitly states this synchronization behavior under synchronous=NORMAL. The claim does not state the power-loss rollback consequence required by normal-durability.

concepts.reason: Claims f1 and f2 establish checkpointing as a distinct WAL operation and define its transfer function.
Claims f3–f8 establish distinct execution, waiting, truncation, and status behaviors internal to checkpointing.
Claims f10–f14 support automatic initiation thresholds, disabling, mode selection, and callback interaction.
Claims f15–f18 establish reader boundaries, saved progress, and starvation as distinct checkpoint mechanisms and limits.
Claims f19–f21 support conditional WAL reuse and final cleanup, distinct from transferring frames into the database.
Claims f22–f26 support synchronization ordering, overhead, and scheduling tradeoffs within checkpointing.
No claim develops reader concurrency as a separate concept. Checkpoint-specific reader interference is already represented by c4; general reader snapshots are outside the internal checkpoint scope.
No claim establishes general writer serialization as a distinct developed idea. General WAL writer concurrency is outside the internal checkpoint scope.
No claim develops rollback journaling, and this alternative journaling mechanism is outside the internal checkpoint scope.

overall_limitations: Several supported claims state only part of a rubric entry; those entries receive no gold credit.
The output omits checkpoint-lock contention, busy-handler fallback, detailed status counters, multi-database behavior, per-connection configuration scope, and checkpoint-induced commit latency.
The skipped neighboring concepts are named but not developed through claims.
No exact claim duplicates were identified; related claims often supply different conditions or consequences.
